overview: I study planning and decision making in operations and supply chain systems. My work combines mathematical programming, decomposition, adaptive search and AI with questions about how limited resources should be assigned, how activities should be scheduled and how decisions should be coordinated across a system.

The research is organized around three connected concerns: coordination between operating stages, adaptation when conditions change, and computational methods that make these decisions tractable. Published studies in ports, cross-docking and shipping provide a foundation; my broader interests include industrial and service operations, healthcare and humanitarian logistics, energy use and public infrastructure.

algorithms.question: How can mathematical structure, algorithms and learning be combined to support complex decisions?
paragraphs: Operational decisions often combine assignment, sequencing, timing and shared-capacity constraints. I develop mathematical formulations and algorithms that use this structure: compact mixed-integer models, decomposition into linked subproblems, exact improvement within heuristic search, and adaptive selection of search operators. The central question is which parts of a problem need to be solved jointly and which can be separated without losing feasibility or useful coordination.

My published work includes compact berth-scheduling formulations, Benders decomposition and column generation, as well as hyperheuristics that combine adaptive search with exact optimization. Ongoing interests extend to learning-guided resource allocation and scheduling in industrial and service systems.

I am also interested in how language models can assist with operating rules, mathematical formulation and algorithm design. Solver feedback provides a way to test feasibility, identify inconsistent assumptions and evaluate proposed search strategies. These ideas require comparisons with established methods, with explicit attention to solution quality, computation time and the reliability of the resulting decisions.

maritime.question: How should decisions be coordinated across facilities, organizations and stages of an operating system?
paragraphs: A facility schedule is part of a larger operating system. Inbound arrivals determine when equipment, labor, processing capacity and storage are needed; decisions inside the facility determine outbound availability and service. My research examines how these interdependencies should be represented and when joint planning produces value over separately optimized decisions.

Questions include when processing or storage becomes the dominant bottleneck, whether capacity at one stage can substitute for capacity elsewhere, and how investments in equipment should be coordinated with operating policies. Ports and distribution facilities are important applications, alongside manufacturing, inventories, healthcare logistics and other service operations.

Electrification and automation add further dependencies. Charging time, electricity availability, equipment compatibility and safe operating sequences can change usable capacity. I am interested in models that connect these requirements with adoption decisions, service reliability, energy use and cost.

resilience.question: How can systems remain useful, adaptable and sustainable when conditions and priorities change?
paragraphs: Disruption changes more than the input to a schedule: it can remove feasible actions, shift bottlenecks and make established commitments difficult to keep. I study how operating plans can be revised when resources, demand or access change, and how the benefit of a new plan should be weighed against the cost of changing the old one.

This connects recovery with preparedness. Where should reserve capacity, inventory, schedule slack or alternative resources be placed before a disruption? Which decisions can be preserved afterward, and which must be reconsidered together? My interests include production and distribution networks, humanitarian logistics, emergency response and public services.

Sustainability introduces related trade-offs between service, cost, energy and environmental performance. Work on ship schedule recovery, rail-crossing decisions and circular supply chains informs this direction. Current interests also include whether electrification investments translate into actual equipment use and how resource-allocation decisions can account for multiple types of consequences.

cases.title: A smaller model for berth scheduling
cases.summary: A compact berth-scheduling formulation supports Benders decomposition and column generation for larger planning problems.
cases.question: How can a berth-scheduling model remain operationally useful without carrying unnecessary variables and constraints?
cases.approach: This study develops a mixed-integer formulation for dynamic, discrete berth scheduling. Two-dimensional decision variables and a simplified vessel-sequencing structure reduce model complexity. Benders decomposition and column generation build on the formulation to address larger instances.
cases.evidence: The computational study compares the formulation with five mathematical models and three metaheuristics. It reports solutions for instances with more than 260 vessels within two hours under the tested settings, alongside sensitivity analysis of operational parameters.
cases.meaning: The study connects formulation design with algorithm design: reducing mathematical overhead can make more demanding berth-planning instances accessible to exact optimization methods.
cases.connection: Model design and decomposition are relevant wherever connected assignments and sequencing decisions make a planning problem difficult.

cases.title: Coordinating inbound and outbound trucks
cases.summary: Sequential optimization and pricing-guided search address coupled truck services, freight transfers and departure timing.
cases.question: How can inbound unloading, internal freight transfer and outbound loading be scheduled together?
cases.approach: The study formulates coordinated truck service as a mixed-integer linear program. Its objective accounts for waiting, handling, temporary storage and delay costs. A sequential fix-and-optimize framework constructs service plans in batches that respect precedence relationships; a second framework uses pricing-guided search.
cases.evidence: The paper evaluates the model and the two solution frameworks through computational experiments and sensitivity analysis. These experiments examine solution approaches for different computational settings and the operational consequences of scheduling parameters.
cases.meaning: The work treats a cross-dock as a connected set of services. Optimizing one truck or door in isolation can miss the timing relationships that determine whether the full plan is feasible.
cases.connection: The broader question is how local scheduling decisions should be coordinated across processing, transfer and service stages.

cases.title: Learning which scheduling operators to use
cases.summary: Thompson Sampling adapts operator selection while repair and exact evaluation address schedule feasibility and accuracy.
cases.question: Can a truck-scheduling search procedure learn which operators are useful as the search progresses?
cases.approach: The Hybridized Thompson Sampling Hyperheuristic combines evolutionary search with an adaptive operator-selection controller. A repair-and-penalty mechanism handles inbound–outbound precedence constraints. Fast approximate fitness evaluation supports exploration, while exact optimization refines schedule evaluation.
cases.evidence: On the reported benchmark instances, the algorithm produces solutions comparable with exact optimization for small problems and improves on the comparison metaheuristics. The paper reports improvements of up to approximately 24% and an average runtime of 186.71 seconds across its experimental setting.
cases.meaning: The study connects adaptive operator learning with the feasibility and evaluation requirements of a terminal schedule. The approach uses different evaluation strategies during exploration and refinement to manage computation time and solution accuracy.
cases.connection: Learning to choose search strategies raises questions about algorithm adaptation and transfer across operating conditions and decision problems.

cases.title: Combining adaptive search with exact optimization
cases.summary: A berth-scheduling hyperheuristic adapts genetic operators and periodically applies problem-specific exact improvement.
cases.question: How can a search algorithm adapt to the berth-scheduling problem while retaining the benefits of exact optimization?
cases.approach: The Hyperheuristic Hybridized with Exact Optimization addresses dynamic, discrete berth allocation and scheduling. It chooses genetic operators according to their observed performance and periodically applies berth-specific exact optimization procedures to improve candidate schedules.
cases.evidence: Computational comparisons examine the algorithm against exact-optimization-inspired methods and established metaheuristics. Component experiments investigate the contribution of hyperheuristic control and hybridization. Scenario analysis considers berth availability, vessel arrival intensity and departure-delay penalties.
cases.meaning: This study is part of my work on algorithms that adapt their search behavior while using the structure of the application. It connects flexible search with the explicit timing and assignment decisions in terminal planning.
cases.connection: The broader interest is how flexible search can use exact optimization and application structure within the same algorithm.

cases.title: Evaluating rail-crossing closure decisions
cases.summary: An optimization framework considers safety, economic and environmental effects alongside delay and maintenance costs.
cases.question: Which level crossings should be considered for closure when several types of consequences must be evaluated together?
cases.approach: The study develops an optimization model that includes safety, economic and environmental benefits as well as traffic-delay and maintenance implications. A sorting-inspired heuristic addresses the resulting decision problem. Computational experiments use crossings in Florida.
cases.evidence: The paper compares the heuristic with an exact solution method and examines the sensitivity of closure decisions to model inputs. The associated FDOT project also produced a final technical report, linking this research to a broader decision-support investigation.
cases.meaning: The work frames closure selection as a system-level allocation decision. Its value is in evaluating multiple consequences consistently, rather than recommending closure solely from one indicator.
cases.connection: This study connects to a wider interest in public resource allocation when safety, economic and environmental consequences must be considered together.

cases.title: Recovering ship schedules under environmental constraints
cases.summary: Multi-objective optimization examines the tension between schedule recovery, monetary losses and speed-reduction incentives.
cases.question: How should a shipping line recover from disruption when sailing faster conflicts with environmental rules or incentives?
cases.approach: This collaborative study models monetary losses and port-arrival delays as competing objectives. It incorporates voluntary speed-reduction incentive programs, emission-control requirements and multiple recovery options. The solution method combines dynamic secant approximation with an epsilon-constraint approach.
cases.evidence: Computational experiments use the South East Asia Pendulum shipping route, with sensitivity analysis exploring how different settings affect recovery choices.
cases.meaning: The study makes the conflict explicit: a strategy that reduces arrival delay may sacrifice a speed-compliance incentive or increase cost. Examining alternative solutions supports a more informed recovery decision than optimizing one objective alone.
cases.connection: The wider research question is how to revise operating plans while balancing service, cost and environmental objectives.

approach: My teaching emphasizes a progression from mathematical understanding to independent application and reasoning. Students should be able to explain why a method is appropriate, state its assumptions and interpret what its output means.

In optimization and computational work, that progression can start with a small example that students can inspect by hand, move to implementation, and then ask them to compare approaches on a less structured problem. Validation and interpretation are part of the task, alongside obtaining a numerical answer.

I aim to maintain common learning expectations while providing different entry points for students with different preparation. Guided examples, targeted review and intermediate project submissions can help students move toward more independent work.
teaching.mentoring: I have mentored undergraduate and master’s researchers and served as an external master’s thesis committee member. My approach emphasizes a clear research question, careful computational work and the ability to explain a result and its limitations.

agenda.title: Coordinating operations across facilities and organizations
agenda.text: I plan to study how sourcing, processing, storage, distribution and service decisions should be coordinated when they share resources or depend on one another in time. Questions include where bottlenecks emerge, when extra capacity can substitute for better coordination, and how decision authority and information sharing affect the value of joint planning. Mathematical models and decomposition methods can connect local operating decisions with system-wide performance.

agenda.title: Preparedness, recovery and the stability of operating plans
agenda.text: My interests include choosing flexibility before disruption and using it effectively afterward. Reserve resources, alternative sourcing and inventory buffers need to be considered alongside rescheduling and reassignment policies. I aim to examine when existing commitments should be protected, how the cost of changing a plan affects recovery, and how decisions at one stage influence the rest of a network.

agenda.title: Learning and language models for mathematical optimization
agenda.text: I am interested in learning-guided search, adaptive allocation of computation and language-model assistance with formulation and algorithm development. A useful planning system must connect domain knowledge with mathematical feasibility and measurable operating objectives. I plan to investigate feedback between AI systems and optimization solvers, including how to detect modeling errors, compare proposed strategies and communicate the consequences of a solution.

agenda.title: Electrification, automation and sustainable operations
agenda.text: Equipment investment creates operating value only when supporting infrastructure, schedules and organizational practices permit effective use. I am interested in joint investment and operating models for electric fleets, charging systems and automated handling. Relevant outcomes include capital and operating cost, service reliability, energy demand, emissions and the distribution of transition costs across organizations.

agenda.title: Service systems and emerging computational methods
agenda.text: Healthcare scheduling, emergency operations and public services provide settings in which limited resources, service commitments and changing conditions interact. I am interested in extending structured optimization and adaptive solution methods to these systems. A complementary exploratory interest concerns quantum and classical hybrid optimization, including which problem structures are suitable and how to compare methods under a common computational budget.

currentWork.title: Integrated scheduling and shared-resource allocation
currentWork.text: Current studies connect local task sequences with fleet coordination, handling capacity and reusable resources. They examine how processing and movement decisions affect system completion, resource requirements and energy use. The broader goal is to identify useful decompositions while retaining the timing relationships that make a complete operating plan feasible.

currentWork.title: Emergency response and healthcare scheduling
currentWork.text: I am studying resource-constrained planning in flood response and healthcare services. These settings involve coupled movement, service and capacity decisions under limited time for computation. The methodological questions concern compact representations, rolling planning and selective revision of decisions when conditions or computational budgets change.

currentWork.title: Infrastructure electrification and implementation
currentWork.text: Work on shore power examines the connection between infrastructure commitments, project readiness, equipment capability and actual use. The research asks what evidence is needed to assess implementation and how operating activity should inform investment priorities and environmental reporting.

currentWork.title: Source-grounded AI for operational knowledge
currentWork.text: I have developed a local prototype for retrieving and synthesizing information from public transportation-agency manuals. The work explores how technical guidance can be made easier to find and interpret with source references. It complements my interest in connecting domain knowledge with optimization; it remains a research prototype rather than an agency decision system.
